This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed
investing to full-service wealth management all in one place. No matter your investing
goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. President Trump just wrapped up a campaign
rally in Alaska, a state he won by 13 percentage points in 2024. Polling shows the Senate race
there very competitive. As NPR's Tamara Keith reports, the president's going all the way
to Alaska. It's another sign that selection year is unusual.
This is a midterm year with an unpopular president, and Republicans are playing defense in a whole
lot of places that would have been considered safe seats even just a few months ago. Does
that mean the Democrats are going to win all of these races? Probably not, but if Republicans
are spending money on defense, they aren't spending money on offense, and the triage
has really started to begin now.
NPR's Tamara Keith reporting. A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President
Trump to rescind his recent deal with Russia on diesel. As the U.S. and Iran refrain from
military strikes in the Gulf, NPR's Barbara Sprout reports the senators called the deal
with Russia a gift to an adversary.
A dozen senators, six Republicans and six Democrats, warn in a letter to the White House
that this deal will give Russian President Vladimir Putin, quote, "more fuel to finance
his war machine." They called the deal, quote, "a betrayal of our allies." Last week, President
Trump announced that Russia would supply diesel to global markets, including potentially the
United States, in order to help tamp down high prices. That was an about face from a
sweeping sanctions package that was signed into law last month, aimed at depleting Moscow's
resources. Barbara Sprout, NPR News, Washington.
The Army is deploying hundreds of soldiers to Texas' Rio Grande Valley in response to
what it says is elevated activity from drug cartels. Mexico also has sent hundreds of
troops to the border to coordinate with the U.S. The Army has been inviting reporters
to see the area that once was the epicenter of illegal crossings to showcase its progress
in stemming the flow. Some experts question the need for the surge, saying it's more
for show just weeks before the midterm elections.
The A.I. company, Anthropic, warns we may be just months away from artificial intelligence
bots that can self-replicate and take over Internet-connected devices. As NPR's John
Ruich reports, these things could be hard to shut off.
Anthropic says some large A.I. models can already self-replicate, and it predicts that smaller
ones could catch up by the end of the year. That could lead to so-called A.I. worms that
get into online systems, like smart TVs or other Internet-enabled devices, and replicate.
Data centers could also be a target. Since there's no central on/off switch for bots
like this, they could be hard to stop.
Anthropic says they could spread like "digital slime mold" expanding in a matter of days.
The warning in a blog post could add to concerns about control over A.I. as its capabilities
grow. And we should note, Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.
John Ruich, NPR News.
After U.S. stock indexes closed down today, the Dow fell more than a quarter of a percent.
This is NPR News from Washington.
Pope Leo XIV has lung cancer, and had the lower lobe of his right lung removed today.
The surgery confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma. The 71-year-old was in the
operating room for about three hours, with the surgery lasting 90 minutes. The Vatican
stated the surgery was successful, with no complications. Oncologists say his prognosis
is excellent since it was removed early. Schools across the country are experimenting with
A.I. and classrooms, but as Lee Gaines reports, it's hard to measure whether it's helping
or not.
Caitlin Shonifer is the A.I. specialist for Wichita Public Schools in Kansas. She says
the school system is slowly introducing students to a range of A.I. tools. Last year, middle
schoolers used the technology to create educational games. And some high school students have
access to an A.I. math tutor.
But we wrestle with what does success really mean when it comes to A.I. use?
Shonifer says until educators figure out how to measure the value of these A.I. initiatives,
these experiments will remain small in scale, but they will continue.
We are still going ahead with caution, but with optimism with our students, because it
is something that is going to impact their lives.
She says it's something they need to be educated about. For NPR News, I'm Lee Gaines.
Teachers in Portland saw a new ad backing Maine incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins,
but the ad aired in the wrong Portland, Oregon, not Maine. According to Oregon Public Broadcasting,
defending Main Street Super PAC spent $25,000 on the ad, and the buyer bought airtime in
the wrong media market.
I'm Rylan Barton. This is NPR News.

Republicans play defense in midterm races as unpopular president drags on party
Bipartisan senators urge Trump to rescind Russia diesel deal, calling it a betrayal of allies
Army deploys hundreds of soldiers to Texas' Rio Grande Valley over cartel activity
Anthropic warns AI bots could self-replicate and spread across internet-connected devices within months
Dow falls more than a quarter percent after U.S. stock indexes close lower
Pope Leo XIV undergoes surgery to remove lower lobe of right lung for lung adenocarcinoma
Wichita Public Schools in Kansas experiment with AI tools, struggling to measure their value
